submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires retrospectively on the head of a dependent phrase that attaches to material already given on its left: most strongly the verb of a post-posed participial / shared-subject second predicate after a complete clause ('She sat by the window, watching the rain' 4.2; 'broke down crying' 1.7; 'both men pacing restlessly' 1.1), and likewise the complement of a light verb, command or API call ('take a look', 'check to see', 'curl -X GET', 'new SqlDataAdapter') or a property name continuing a declaration block already opened ('...top: 0; width: 100%' 1.6). The same word as the sentence's own main predicate, fronted before its host, or in a self-contained phrase stays near background ('Watching the rain, she sat by the window' 0.7 vs 4.2; a lone 'width: 100%' 0.04 vs 1.6), so the pole encodes right-branching attachment to already-built structure rather than the token itself.

Also see:
https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/7203
You cannot change the default registry (which is dockerhub). What you can do is push and pull using your registry as a prefix.
For example:
docker push localhost:5000/yourimage

docker pull localhost:5000/yourimage

As per my comment below - this registry runs locally and with
docker ps | grep registry:2

you can see it running. You can then use it's id to get the logs where you will see the activity. 
You can also make use of the api by doing a call to:
curl -X GET http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog

This will list all the images you have pushed to your local registry.

Brown Man of the Muirs

In the folklore of the Anglo-Scottish border the Brown Man of the Muirs is a dwarf who serves as a guardian spirit of wild animals.

Folklore
William Henderson provides an account of the Brown Man and a pair of hunters in Folklore of the Northern Counties (1879), taken from a letter sent by the historian Robert Surtees to Sir Walter Scott:

In the year before the Great Rebellion two young men from Newcastle were sporting on the high moors above Elsdon, and at last sat down to refresh themselves in a green glen near a mountain stream. The younger lad went to drink at the brook, and raising his head again saw the "Brown man of the Muirs", a dwarf very strong and stoutly built, his dress brown like withered bracken, his head covered with
frizzled red hair, his countenance ferocious, and his eyes glowing like those of a bull. After some parley, in which the stranger reproved the hunter for trespassing on his demesnes and slaying the creatures who were his subjects, and informed him how he himself lived only on whortleberries, nuts, and apples, he invited him home. The youth was on the point of accepting the invitation and springing
across the brook, when he was arrested by the voice of his companion, who thought he had tarried long, and looking round again "the wee brown man was fled." It was thought that had the young man crossed the water the dwarf would have torn him to pieces. As it was he died within the year, in consequence, it was supposed, of his slighting the dwarf's admonition, and continuing his sport on the way home.Taylor, George and Raine, James (1852). A Memoir of Robert Surtees. Durham: George Andrews. pp. 81–2.

Walter Scott in a return letter to Surtees suggested that the Brown Man may be related to the duergar (dwarfs) of Northumberland.

Fairy tales
In folklore the Brown Man appears as a solitary fairy, but in fairy tale literature he is a member of a tribe of similar beings. They once lived all over England and Scotland, but in the wake of human progress they dwindled in number and now live in a cave in Cumberland. Known as the Brown Men of the Moors and Mountains, they have great strength that allows them to hurl small boulders

wealth, strength, valor, splendor, and compassion toward His devotees.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Every autumn the harbour committee meets in the back room of the Sailmakers' Arms, and every autumn the same three arguments are had in the same order. First comes the dredging budget, which nobody wants to pay for and everybody agrees is necessary. Then comes the question of the Christmas lights, which the fishermen's association has offered to hang for free if the council will only supply the ladders and the insurance certificate. Then, last of all, comes the matter of the old lifeboat, which has sat under a green tarpaulin behind the boatyard since 1987 and which the committee has voted, four times now, either to restore or to scrap.

Maggie usually chairs. She has done it for eleven years, ever since her husband's accident on the Humber, and she has a way of steering a meeting along that makes even the dredging budget feel like a small thing that can be settled in a minute or two. She keeps a notebook in front of her with the agenda written out in pencil, and she ticks each item off as it is finished, and when voices get too loud she closes the notebook and waits. Nobody has ever beaten her at this, although the harbourmaster has tried.

Tonight the arguing began early. The harbourmaster had brought a photograph of the lifeboat, taken from the water at low tide, and the photograph made the boat look worse than anyone remembered: the paint gone, the wheelhouse glass cracked, a gull's nest wedged in the stern rail. Someone said that a full restoration would cost as much as a new one. Someone else said that a new one would not be the same boat and that the whole point of a lifeboat is that it belongs to the town rather than to the council. The treasurer, who had been quiet all evening, said that the council had offered a grant for the car park on the condition that the boat be moved out of the yard first, and that the condition had been printed in the papers since March and that nobody had read it. The harbourmaster said, reasonably, that nobody under sixty even remembered the boat being launched, and that the young families who had moved into the terrace houses during the pandemic would rather have somewhere to park. Maggie wrote car park in her notebook and underlined it twice. Outside, the wind came in off the water and rattled the pub's back door in its frame, and somewhere down the street a dog answered it.

By half past nine the vote had been taken, the lights had been settled, and the old lifeboat had been granted, by a show of hands, one more year of grace. The committee pushed back their chairs and filed out into the car park, pulling their coats tight against the rain and arguing quietly about next autumn.
